keyVerseText: And he shall offer of the sacrifice of the peace offering an offering made by fire unto the LORD; the fat thereof, and the whole rump, it shall he take off hard by the backbone; and the fat that covereth the inwards, and all the fat that is upon the inwards,
rootMeaning: The root of עָצֶה (ʻâtseh) is עָצָה (ʻâtsâh), which primarily means 'to shut' or 'to fasten firmly.' This etymology suggests a sense of closure or firmness, which enriches the noun's meaning beyond a mere anatomical term. Instead of simply referring to a bone, it conveys the idea of a structural support that holds or secures, emphasizing strength and stability inherent in the spine or backbone.
usageInScripture: This Hebrew noun appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Leviticus 3:9, where it is translated as 'by the backbone.' The singular occurrence and consistent translation highlight its precise anatomical reference to the spine or sacrum, underscoring the importance of this part of the animal in sacrificial contexts. The limited usage emphasizes the word's specialized role in describing a key part of the peace offering.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עָצֶה as the backbone or spine, the structural support of the body, offers profound theological insight into God's design and order. The backbone symbolizes strength, firmness, and support, reflecting how God upholds creation by His power. In the sacrificial system, the emphasis on the backbone may point to the completeness and integrity required in offerings to the Lord, prefiguring Christ who is the 'backbone' or foundation of the church. This word reminds believers that faith is not fragile but firmly anchored in the unshakable support of God's grace.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 3:9 instructs the offerer to remove the fat and the whole rump 'hard by the backbone,' highlighting the significance of this part of the sacrifice. The use of עָצֶה here directs attention to the precise location, underscoring the importance of offering the best and most substantial parts to God. This detail enriches our understanding of worship as one that involves careful obedience and reverence, offering not just any portion but what is structurally central and vital.
